Reminder

# Page 7^page=7
First rank tensors Covariant and contravariant - ˝rst-rank tensors In a generalised coordinate system in 3D, a ˝rst-rank tensor (i.e. a vector) A is uniquely determined either by its three covariant components Ai, its three contravariant components Ai Covariant and contravariant components are related: Ai = gikAk, Ai = gikAk where gik and gik are determined by the basis of the coordinate system . 4 24

# Page 8^page=8
Second-rank tensors - covariant and con- travariant components Second-rank tensors - covariant and contravariant components In dimension 3D, a second rank tensor is speci˝ed by its nine components, which can be covariant Aik, contravariant Aik, mixed A.k i , Ai .k. 5 24

# Page 9^page=9
Second-rank tensors - Notation of mixed components Notation Notice that the mixed components are denoted with dots: A ·k i and Ai ·k. The dot in the mixed components emphasizes the order of occurrence of the indices. For instance, in A·k i , the ˝rst index is covariant" and the second contravariant": “A·k i = (Ai) k” while in Ai ·k, the ˝rst index is contravariant" and the second covariant"': “Ai ·k = (Ai)k”. 6 24

# Page 10^page=10
Second-rank tensors - transformations Second-rank tensors - transformations The components are transformed via: A′ ik = L ℓ i′L m k′ Aℓm, A′ik = L i′ ℓ L k′ mA ℓm, A ′·k i = L ℓ i′L k′ mA·m ℓ , A ′i ·k = L i′ ℓ L m k′ A ℓ ·m, where Lk i′ and Lk′ i ( i, k = 1, 2, 3) are the coe˚cients of the direct and the inverse transformations. 7 24

# Page 11^page=11
Second-rank tensors - relations between components Second-rank tensors - relations between components The relations between the various components of a tensor are: Aik = giℓgkmAℓm = gkℓA ·ℓ i = giℓAℓ ·k, A ik = giℓgkmAℓm = giℓA.k ℓ = gkℓAi .ℓ, A.k i = gkℓAiℓ = giℓAℓk, Ai .k = giℓAℓk = gkℓAiℓ. 8 24

# Page 12^page=12
Second-rank tensors  Symmetry and Antisymmetry Second-rank tensors  Symmetry and Antisymmetry Symmetry and antisymmetry apply only to pairs of indices in the same positions: A··ℓ ik is symmetric in i and k if A ··ℓ ik = A··ℓ ki . Bik ··ℓ is anti-symmetric in i and k if Bik ··ℓ = −Bki ··ℓ. 9 24

# Page 13^page=13
Indices in different positions Indices in di˙erent positions Last week, we showed that if Ai is a covariant tensor and Bi is a contravariant tensor, then Ai + Bi does not form a tensor. 10 24

# Page 14^page=14
Associated tensors

# Page 15^page=15
Lowering indices Lowering indices Given a tensor, we can derive other tensors by raising or lowering indices . For instance, given the tensor Apq, by raising the index p, we obtain the tensor A p ·q. (The dot indicates the original position of the moved index.) By raising the index q as well, we obtain A pq ·· . Remark: Sometimes the dots might be omitted. 11 24

# Page 16^page=16
Deriving new tensors Deriving new tensors These derived tensors can be obtained by forming inner products of the given tensor with the metric tensor gpq or gpq: Ap ·q = grpArq and A·q p = grpArq Rule: On (both) RHS: look for repeated index (in this case r). We then replace this index according to the metric tensor: ▶ grp and grp both mean we replace r with p. Raise or lower the index according to the metric tensor: ▶ grp means we raise p, while ▶ grp means we lower p. 12 24

# Page 17^page=17
Deriving new tensors - Second Example Deriving new tensors - Second Example Another example is Apq = grpgsqArs. Again, we use the rules: On RHS: look for repeated indices (in this case r and s). Replace these indices according to the metric tensor: ▶ grp means replace r with p ▶ and gsq means we replace s with q. Raise or lower the index according to the metric tensor: ▶ grp and gsq mean we raise p and q, respectively. 13 24

# Page 18^page=18
Deriving new tensors - Third Example Deriving new tensors - Third Example We also have A p ·rs = grqA pq ··s On RHS: look for repeated index (in this case q). Replace this index according to the metric tensor: ▶ grq means we replace q with r. Raise or lower the index according to the metric tensor: ▶ grq means we lower r. 14 24

# Page 19^page=19
Deriving new tensors - Last Example Deriving new tensors - Last Example The following holds: A qm.tk ··n = gpkgsngrmAq·st ·r··p Rules: On RHS: look for repeated indices (in this case p, r, and s). Replace these indices according to metric tensors: ▶ gpk means replace p with k, ▶ gsn means replace s with n, and ▶ grm means replace r with m. Raise or lower the index according to the position of the indices in the metric tensor: ▶ gpk and gsq mean we raise k and q, respectively, ▶ gsn means we lower n. 15 24

# Page 20^page=20
Associated tensors Associated tensors All tensors obtained as in the previous slides (by lowering or raising indices) are called associated tensors of the given tensor. Example Ap and Ap are associated tensors. The relation between them is given by Ap = gpqAq or Ap = gpqAq. 16 24

# Page 21^page=21
Associated tensors - Cartesian Coordinates Associated tensors - Cartesian Coordinates For Cartesian coordinates, gpq = { 1, if p = q, 0, if p ̸= q. As we have Ap and Ap are associated tensors with relation given by Ap = gpqAq or Ap = gpqAq. We see that in a Coordinate system, Ap = Ap. This explains why no distinction was made between contravariant and covariant components of a vector earlier. 17 24

# Page 22^page=22
The metric tensor

# Page 23^page=23
Metric Tensor as components of a tensor Metric Tensor as components of a tensor The quantities gik, gik, g.k i are actually the components of a second-rank tensor, called the metric tensor . Let us show that gik is in fact a second-rank tensor. By de˝ntion g′ ik = e ′ i · e ′ k = (L ℓ i′eℓ) · (Lm k′ em) = L ℓ i′L m k′ (eℓ · em) = L ℓ i′L m k′ gℓm. We obtained that g′ ik = L ℓ i′L m k′ gℓm that is, gik is a tensor of rank 2. 18 24

# Page 24^page=24
Metric Tensor as components of a tensor - Part 2 Metric Tensor as components of a tensor Similarly, g′ik = e ′i · e ′k = L i′ ℓ L k′ m(e ℓ · e m) = L i′ ℓ L k′ mgℓm, g′·k i = e ′ i · e ′k = L ℓ i′L k′ m(eℓ · e m) = L ℓ i′L k′ mg·m ℓ . We then see that gik are the covariant components of some tensor, gik are contravariant components of some tensor, g·k i are mixed components of some tensor. 19 24

# Page 25^page=25
Metric Tensor as components of a tensor - Part 3 Question Are gik, gik, and g·k i components of the same tensor? Let us check To verify that all these quantities are components of the same tensor, we need only show that they are connected by relations of the form Aik = giℓgkmAℓm = gkℓA ·ℓ i = giℓAℓ ·k, A ik = giℓgkmAℓm = giℓA·k ℓ = gkℓAi ·ℓ, A·k i = gkℓAiℓ = giℓAℓk, Ai ·k = giℓAℓk = gkℓAiℓ. 20 24

# Page 26^page=26
Metric Tensor as components of a tensor - Part 4 Metric Tensor as components of the same tensor It follows from the de˝nition of gik and the properties of the basis e1, e2, e3 and its dual e1, e2, e3 that ei = giℓe ℓ. Therefore gik = ei · ek = (giℓe ℓ) · (gkme m) = giℓgkm(e ℓ · e m) = giℓgkmgℓm, gik = ei · ek = (giℓe ℓ) · ek = giℓgℓ ·k, as required. 21 24

# Page 27^page=27
Higher order tensors in gen- eralised coordinates

# Page 28^page=28
Higher order tensors in generalised coordinates Higher order tensors in generalised coordinates In a generalised coordinate system, a tensor of rank n has 3n components. However, it can have various kinds of components. That is, covariant, contravariant and mixed components. 22 24

# Page 29^page=29
Components of higher order tensors in gen- eralised coordinates Example A third-rank tensor has 33 = 27 components. But it has mixed components A··ℓ ik , Ai· ·kℓ, . . . which transform according to the formulae A′··ℓ ik = L m i′ L n k′L ℓ′ r A··r mn, A ′i·ℓ ·k = L i′ mL n k′L ℓ′ r Am·r ·n , etc . Here we say that A··ℓ ik is a mixed tensor with two covariant indices and one contravariant index (and similarly for Ai·ℓ ·k ). 23 24
